composition: Nominal composition is Fe-35Mn-10Al-0.1C (the series is written Fe-35Mn-xAl-0.1C with x = 4, 6, 8, 10 wt% Al; the experimental description additionally lists minor additions of 0.1Nb, 0.1V, 1Mo and 1W). The measured bulk composition of the 10Al steel (Table 1, wet-chemical analysis) is Mn 34.66, Al 10.17, C 0.097, Nb 0.11, V 0.11, Mo 1.30, W 1.38 wt%, Fe balance, matching the nominal 10 wt% Al level. Al partitions strongly into ferrite: the measured ferrite (α) composition is Mn 34.13, Al 10.18 wt%, markedly higher in Al than the coexisting austenite (γ: Mn 37.39, Al 8.51 wt%), which is enriched in Mn. Carbon is not detected in the ferrite of any alloy, nor in the 10Al austenite. The design intent of the Fe-Mn-Al-C system is low density (measured density of the 10Al steel is 6.84 g cm⁻³) with Al added to reduce weight, stabilise ferrite and promote B2/DO3 ordering, Mn acting as the austenite stabiliser, and C contributing both to low density and to short-range ordering in the austenite.
conclusions: As Al increases from 4 to 10 wt% the phase constitution of the Fe-35Mn-xAl-0.1C family transitions from single-phase austenite (4Al) through austenite-matrix duplex (6Al) to ferrite-matrix duplex (8Al) and finally to a nearly fully ferritic 10Al steel, with DO3 ordered domains coexisting inside both the B2 domains and the ferrite and coarsening with Al content. Although the 10Al steel attains the highest yield strength (585 MPa), its elongation collapses to ~4.6 %, i.e. it is brittle; the degradation in plasticity is attributed to the coarsening of DO3 ordered domains and the formation of 18R martensite, together with a ferritic dislocation structure dominated by a few localised long straight screw dislocations that promotes stress concentration and plastic instability. This makes the 10Al steel the contrast case to the 8Al ferrite-based duplex steel, in which the synergistic activity of edge dislocations and dynamic slip band refinement in the ferrite (mitigated by the surrounding austenite) delivers the best strength-ductility balance. The work thus reveals a new ductility-enhancing mechanism for ferrite + austenite duplex steel and provides a route for designing BCC-based low-density steels with high strength and high ductility.
mechanisms: Increasing Al content stabilises ferrite and drives the γ → α transition: from single-phase austenite at 4 %Al to ferrite-matrix duplex at 8 %Al and nearly fully ferritic at 10 %Al, with Al partitioning preferentially into the ferrite (α: 10.18 wt% Al vs γ: 8.51 wt% Al in the 10Al steel).

Al promotes B2/DO3 ordering in the ferrite: B2 and DO3 superlattice reflections appear together along [110]α // [110]DO3, and the DO3 ordered domains — which coexist within both the B2 domains and the ferrite matrix — enlarge progressively with Al content (≈2.0 nm in 6Al, ≈2.1 nm in 8Al, ≈19 nm in 10Al), the intensity of the superlattice spots and the domain size both being greatest at 10 %Al.

Because APB energy in Fe-Al alloys increases with Al content, the anti-phase-boundary-induced attractive force in the 10Al ferrite is substantially stronger than in the 8Al ferrite, producing extremely pronounced dislocation pairing (up to six pairs with spacings as small as ~3 nm), so dislocations must glide in pairs and cannot move independently.

Interaction between dislocations and the DO3 ordered superlattice forces planar slip: HRTEM/IFFT show dislocations composed of many dislocation dipoles that shear the DO3 superlattice along the dislocation line and slip plane, leaving APBs whose attractive force locks dislocations into pairs and suppresses cross-slip, so both edge and screw dislocations show distinct planar slip.

Unlike the 8Al steel, the large DO3 ordered domains in the 10Al ferrite cannot be completely sheared by dislocations (whereas those in 8Al can), which is consistent with the shear-zone size estimated from paired-dislocation counts (≈3.0 nm in 10Al, far below the TEM-observed ≈19 nm; in 8Al the estimate ≈1.5 nm matches the TEM value ≈2.1 nm) — the unshearable coarse domains correlate with embrittlement.

The 10Al ferrite deforms predominantly by a small number of long straight, non-uniformly distributed screw dislocations (Burgers vector a/2[111]); screw dislocations are energetically favoured over edge dislocations in Fe-Al ordered alloys, and their sparse, localised activation causes stress concentration, plastic instability and brittle fracture (as also reported in TiZrHfNb0.4 BCC HEA).

Acicular 18R martensite forms within the ferrite during oil quenching, significantly enriched in Mn and C and depleted in Al; this type of martensite can markedly reduce the ductility of ferrite, contributing to the catastrophic loss of elongation in the 10Al steel.

The austenite of the 10Al steel exhibits L1₂-type short-range order and spinodal decomposition (Al and C concentration fluctuations) revealed by satellite spots near the γ reflections; combined with carbon-induced suppression of cross-slip and the ordered structure, this leads to complex planar slip in the austenite during early deformation rather than the dislocation cell-block structure typical of low-Al lightweight steels.

The coarsening of DO3 ordered domains together with 18R martensite formation is the proposed cause of the plasticity degradation of the 10Al steel, explaining why yield strength keeps rising with Al (to 585 MPa) while total elongation collapses to ~4.6 %.
microstructure: After solution treatment and oil quenching the 10Al steel is nearly fully ferritic: XRD gives 98.1 % ferrite (BCC, quasi-equiaxed grains) and 1.9 % austenite (FCC), the austenite appearing as only a few isolated small regions in the EBSD phase map (red on an almost entirely blue ferrite field). Within the ferrite, selected-area diffraction along [110]α // [110]DO3 shows both B2 and DO3 superlattice reflections (h,k,l all even belong to B2 and DO3; all odd to DO3 only), and the superlattice spots of the 10Al steel are the most intense of the three ferrite patterns examined. Paired dark-field images from the {111}DO3 and {002}DO3 reflections show that DO3 ordered domains coexist both within the B2 ordered domains and within the ferrite matrix, with a maximum DO3 domain size estimated by TEM at approximately 19 nm — the largest of the series and evidence that Al promotes DO3 domain coarsening. Acicular/needle-shaped precipitates are present inside the ferrite grains and are identified as 18R martensite formed during quenching; TEM EDS mapping shows them significantly enriched in Mn and C while depleted in Al. The small austenite fraction exhibits L1₂-type short-range ordered (SRO) domains and concentration fluctuations of Al and C (spinodal decomposition on quenching), revealed by satellite spots near the γ reflections in the [100]γ SADP. After ~3 % engineering strain the ferrite contains predominantly long, straight, non-uniformly (localised) distributed screw dislocations, with only a small number of long straight dislocations activated and a few mixed dislocations; all dislocation types exhibit distinct planar slip, and dislocation pairing is extremely pronounced (up to six pairs, spacings as small as ~3 nm). The ferrite Burgers vector is a/2[111], confirmed by g·b = 0 analysis near the [111] zone axis. The austenite in the 10Al steel shows complex planar slip in the early deformation stage.
processing: The processing lineage is: (1) vacuum induction melting of ingots under a high-purity Ar atmosphere; (2) homogenization of the as-cast ingots at 1150 °C for 4 h; (3) hot forging into rods of 16.5 mm diameter; and (4) solution treatment of the bars at 1050 °C for 2 h followed by oil quenching, the step that defines this sample and yields a microstructure with nearly equiaxed grains (the four solution-treated steels are designated 4Al, 6Al, 8Al and 10Al). No atmosphere, cooling rate or reduction ratio is reported for the forging step. Tensile specimens (5 mm diameter, 25 mm gauge length) were machined from the quenched rods with the tensile axis parallel to the rod axis. Interrupted tensile tests to engineering strains of 3 %, 10 %, 20 % and 28 % were used to track deformation microstructures; because of its plastic instability, the 10Al steel could only be examined in the deformed state at ~3 % engineering strain.
properties: Tensile testing at room temperature in air at 1.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ (MTS machine, standard specimens 5 mm diameter × 25 mm gauge length, axis parallel to the rod axis; at least three specimens per condition) gives the 10Al steel a yield strength of 585 (±29) MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 613 (±41) MPa, uniform elongation of 2.1 (±1.1) % and total elongation of 4.6 (±1.6) %. It thus has the highest yield strength but the lowest ductility of the four steels, failing in a brittle manner (its engineering stress-strain curve rises steeply and terminates at very small strain, before ~0.05). Microhardness rises with Al content, ferrite reaching just below ~330 HV at 10 wt% Al while austenite reaches just under ~210 HV, confirming ferrite as the strengthening phase (ferrite microhardness is significantly higher than that of austenite). The measured density is 6.84 g cm⁻³. Characterization techniques applied across the study and to this steel include SEM/EBSD phase mapping (JSM-7800F, 1 μm step, HKL Channel 5), TEM in bright field, selected-area diffraction, dark-field imaging, HRTEM and IFFT (FEI Tecnai G2 F20 and Talos F200X at 200 kV), XRD for phase mass fractions, EPMA for phase compositions, TEM-EDS elemental mapping, wet-chemical analysis, Archimedes density measurement, Vickers microhardness and room-temperature tensile testing. The room-temperature stacking-fault energy of austenite is reported for the 4Al, 6Al and 8Al steels but no value is given for the 10Al austenite.
summary: 10Al steel is the highest-aluminium member (10 wt% Al) of the Fe-35Mn-xAl-0.1C (x = 4, 6, 8, 10 wt%) low-density steel family studied for its microstructure-mechanical property relationship. Prepared by vacuum induction melting, homogenization at 1150 °C/4 h, hot forging to 16.5 mm rods and solution treatment at 1050 °C/2 h followed by oil quenching, it is nearly a fully ferritic (BCC) steel — 98.1 % ferrite and only 1.9 % austenite by mass — whose ferrite carries B2 and DO3 ordered domains plus acicular 18R martensite. It shows the highest yield strength of the series (585 MPa) but collapses to about 4.6 % total elongation, exhibiting brittle behaviour; the paper uses it as the Al-rich end-member that contrasts with the ductile 8Al ferrite-based duplex steel.
unmapped: Table 2 reports the room-temperature stacking-fault energy of austenite for 4Al (51.25), 6Al (62.64) and 8Al (68.47 mJ m⁻²) but gives an en-dash for 10Al_γ, i.e. no γ_SFE value exists for the 10Al steel, consistent with it being nearly fully ferritic.

The multi-stage strain-hardening analysis (stages A–E, flow-stress decomposition σ(ε) = 0.757σ_α(ε) + 0.243σ_γ(ε), Table 4, Fig. 6, Fig. 9) is developed for and quantitatively applied to the 8Al steel, not to the 10Al steel; in the 10Al steel the strain-hardening-rate curve falls to zero within a very small strain.

Some interface-related statements in the paper (edge dislocations readily activated at grain boundaries, and the ~24.3 % austenite acting as a soft phase that alleviates stress localisation) are established for the 8Al steel and are explicitly not attributed to the 10Al steel, which contains only 1.9 % austenite.

The paper contains an internal inconsistency in the nominal composition notation: the title/abstract use Fe-35Mn-xAl-0.1C while the experimental section writes Fe-35Mn-xAl-1C-0.1Nb-0.1V-1Mo-1W; the measured bulk carbon in all alloys (0.076–0.097 wt%) is close to 0.1 wt%.
The tensile-specimen description states the rods were 'water-quenched' whereas the processing description specifies oil quenching after solution treatment at 1050 °C/2 h.
